msg: The third section of Paper 126 deals with Jesus' fifteenth year. That year, while carrying his responsibilities as head of the family, Jesus pondered his mission deeply. He discovered the phrase “⟦Q 126:3.6⟧Son of Man⟦/Q⟧” in the Book of Enoch and began to connect it with his mission, and he was perplexed between the Jewish expectations of the Messiah and the Father's will as he sensed it. Today's passage shows one important attitude Jesus came to learn at that time.

According to the passage, Jesus was learning not to speak of all his thoughts, not to present all his ideas to the world, not even to his own mother. From this year on, his disclosures about what was going on in his mind steadily diminished. He talked less about things an average person could not grasp and which would lead to his being regarded as peculiar. This was neither secretiveness nor hypocrisy. Jesus was learning the wisdom of sharing only as much as people could receive. Mary expected her son to become the Messiah who would restore the throne of David, and had Jesus poured out all his spiritual understanding amid such expectations, it would only have deepened misunderstanding and conflict. Sharing truth, too, has its time and its measure.

But the passage does not hide the loneliness that came with this attitude. To all appearances he became commonplace and conventional, though he did long for someone who could understand his problems. He craved a trustworthy and confidential friend, but his problems were too complex for his human associates to comprehend. So he was compelled to bear his burdens alone. This passage shows how genuine Jesus' humanity was. He felt lonely, wanted to be understood, and longed for a friend. That the Creator of a universe, as a fifteen-year-old boy, went through the solitude of being understood by no one assures us that he knows our hearts when we are lonely.

How, then, did Jesus endure that loneliness? The same section tells us that he took time for deep meditation and often went up to the hilltop to pray. What he could not confide to people, he confided to his heavenly Father. What his human friends could not understand, the Father understood completely. Solitude led him into deeper communion with the Father. We, too, will meet moments in life when no one fully understands us. Even our closest family and friends do not know all the depths of our hearts. At such times we easily sink into loneliness or try to force everything out in order to be understood. Jesus' example shows another way: to share wisely with people and to bring the deep things to the Father.

This passage also teaches the wisdom of restraint in speech. Saying every thought at once is not honesty. Forcing on someone a truth they are not ready to receive produces hurt and misunderstanding instead. Even in his public life Jesus taught his disciples only as much truth as they could bear. That was consideration born of love. At the same time, we must be sensitive to the loneliness of others. Someone who looks ordinary on the outside may be carrying inwardly a burden they cannot tell anyone. Even if we cannot understand it all, we can be friends who stay by their side.

Today, let us bring the burden in the depths of our hearts to the Father. He understands what people cannot fully understand. And in communion with him we meet the One who shares even the burdens we bear alone.
d247.pr: In a quiet moment today, tell the Father honestly about one burden on your heart that you have never told anyone.

msg: Paper 127 tells of Jesus' adolescent years, from sixteen to twenty. After losing his father, he raised and taught his brothers and sisters as head of a large family. The fourth section deals with his nineteenth year, and today's passage introduces the method of child training Jesus used at home: the positive method of urging the doing of good rather than forbidding evil.

According to the passage, by the beginning of this year Jesus had fully won his mother to the acceptance of his methods of child training, the positive injunction to do good in the place of the older Jewish method of forbidding to do evil. In the Jewish tradition of the time, teaching centered on prohibitions, on what not to do. Many commandments of the law took the form of prohibitions, and children too learned first what they must not do. But in his home and throughout his public-teaching career Jesus invariably employed the positive form of exhortation. Always and everywhere did he say, “⟦Q 127:4.2⟧You shall do this — you ought to do that.⟦/Q⟧” Never did he employ the negative mode of teaching derived from the ancient taboos. The passage explains why: he refrained from placing emphasis on evil by forbidding it, while he exalted the good by commanding its performance.

This holds deep psychological insight. When we are told not to do something, our attention is drawn all the more to the forbidden thing. Prohibition imprints evil on the mind and makes us spend energy avoiding it. An exhortation to do good, on the other hand, fills the mind with what is good and gathers energy in that direction. Turn on the light, and the darkness withdraws of itself. This principle is plainly seen in Jesus' public teaching. He did not merely say, do not hate your enemies; he taught, love your enemies. He transformed the passive rule of not harming others into the positive golden rule of doing to others as you would have them do to you. His religion was not a list of things to avoid but a love to be practiced.

The last sentence of the passage is also meaningful. Prayer time in this household was the occasion for discussing anything and everything relating to the welfare of the family. Prayer was not a formal ritual but a living conversation in which the family shared life together and talked over their problems before God. In that home, faith and daily life were not separated. This teaching offers practical wisdom to parents and teachers today. Instead of telling a child, don't run, try saying, walk slowly; instead of, don't fight, say, share nicely. Even when the content is the same, a positive expression lets the child know clearly what to do and feel encouraged rather than scolded.

This principle also applies to our own spiritual growth. We often press ourselves, concentrating only on breaking bad habits. But when we devote ourselves instead to cultivating good habits, the bad ones lose their place. Change comes when we strive to practice kindness rather than merely struggling to suppress anger, and when we begin some small service rather than blaming our laziness. This principle also changes the way we treat others. One who is used to pointing out others' faults makes those around him shrink, but one who points toward the good and encourages makes those around him grow.
Today, let us set our hearts on the good we should do rather than on what we must not do. A life that exalts the good is the surest way to overcome evil.
d248.pr: Today, change one prohibiting word you say to yourself or others into a positive word urging what is good.

msg: The sixth section of Paper 127 covers Jesus’ twentieth year. During this period he courteously declined Rebecca’s declaration of love, visited Jerusalem, and, as he led his family, was growing into a mature man. Today’s passage lists, one by one, the things Jesus was learning at this time, and so paints a picture of the kind of person he was becoming.

The passage tells us that Jesus is rapidly becoming a man, not just a young man but an adult. He has learned well to bear responsibility, and he knows how to carry on in the face of disappointment. He bears up bravely when his plans are thwarted and his purposes temporarily defeated. He has learned how to be fair and just even in the face of injustice. All of these are things that can be learned only amid the real difficulties of life. The passage goes on to say that he is learning how to adjust his ideals of spiritual living to the practical demands of earthly existence. While he toils earnestly for the attainment of a nearer and immediate goal of necessity, he plans for the achievement of a higher and distant goal of idealism. He has very nearly mastered the technique of utilizing the energy of the spiritual drive to turn the mechanism of material achievement.

One sentence sums all of this up: he is slowly learning how to live the heavenly life while he continues on with the earthly existence. This is the central task of the spiritual life. Some people gaze only at heavenly ideals and neglect their earthly responsibilities; others are so bound up in earthly affairs that they forget the ideals of heaven. Jesus lived a life that wove the two into one. The passage also says that more and more he depends upon the ultimate guidance of his heavenly Father while he assumes the fatherly role of guiding and directing the children of his earth family. He was a son leaning on his Father and, at the same time, a father leading his younger brothers and sisters. The deeper the guidance we receive from above, the wiser the guidance we give to those below.

Finally, the passage says that Jesus was becoming experienced in the skillful wresting of victory from the very jaws of defeat, and that he was learning how to transform the difficulties of time into the triumphs of eternity. Poverty, disappointment, and frustration could not break him. Instead, all of them became the material from which eternal values were shaped. This passage shows that Jesus’ Nazareth years were by no means time wasted while he waited for his public ministry. In those hidden years he mastered the most important skills of being human. And these are skills that all of us who live ordinary daily lives today must learn as well.

Our lives, too, are stretched between ideals and reality. We cherish noble spiritual ideals, yet every day we must answer the demands of earning a living, of family, and of work. When the two seem to collide, the way of Jesus does not ask us to give up either one. It teaches us to embody our spiritual ideals in the work of everyday life. Washing the dishes, doing our jobs, and raising our children are not unrelated to the heavenly life. When we do them with love, with honesty, and as an offering to the Father, that daily life becomes the heavenly life. The Thought Adjuster transforms these ordinary moments into eternal values and preserves them.

Today, let us do the work of earth faithfully while living with a heavenly heart. Even when disappointment and frustration come, let us keep going, and let us learn from Jesus how to transform the difficulties of time into the triumphs of eternity.
d249.pr: Do one ordinary task today as an offering to the Father, and look for its heavenly meaning within it.

msg: Paper 128 covers Jesus’ early manhood, from his twenty-first to his twenty-sixth year. The first section tells of his twenty-first year and shows how, during this period, Jesus came to understand ever more clearly his divinity and his humanity, and the mission that lay before him. Today’s passage tells us what choice he made in the light of that understanding.

According to the passage, the Nazareth carpenter now fully understood the work before him. He knew who he was and why he had come to this earth. Yet he chose to live his human life in the channel of its natural flowing. He did not smooth his path with superhuman powers but chose to live under the same conditions as ordinary people. This choice reveals an astonishing humility. Though he knew himself to be the creator of a universe, he labored in the carpenter shop, sweated to support his family, and endured people’s misunderstanding and contempt. He could have revealed his identity and won honor, or used his powers to escape hardship, but he did not. He walked the human path to the very end.

The passage says that in this choice Jesus is indeed an example to his mortal creatures, and it quotes Paul’s words from the letter to the Philippians: being of the nature of God, he thought it not strange to be equal with God, but he made himself to be of little import and, taking upon himself the form of a creature, was born in the likeness of mankind, and he humbled himself and became obedient to death, even the death of the cross. These words sum up the whole of Jesus’ life.

Before these words Paul urges, “⟦Q 128:1.6⟧Let this mind be in you.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus’ humility is not something merely to admire and pass by; it is a mind we are meant to imitate. It is the mind that does not cling to its own position, abilities, or rights, but willingly lowers itself in order to serve others. Our society calls rising higher success. People strive for more authority, higher positions, and greater recognition. But Jesus showed us the opposite way. The highest of all came down to the lowest place, and through that very lowering he gained the sovereignty of a universe (see Paper 120). In the kingdom of God, greatness is measured by service.

What does it mean, concretely, to have this mind? It means not insisting on being right even when we could prove it, lifting up others in places where we ourselves could be recognized, and using our abilities not for ourselves but to help others. It also means not trying to escape the ordinary conditions of life, but willingly carrying the same burdens as everyone else. That Jesus chose the natural human way is a great comfort to us as well. He did not live under special conditions different from ours; he lived under the same conditions we do. So his victory is a victory possible for us too. The path he walked is a path we can walk as well. Of course, we cannot walk it as perfectly as Jesus did. But we can learn that mind a little more each day. The Thought Adjuster and the Spirit of Truth help and strengthen us every time we choose to humble ourselves and serve.
Today, let us look at the positions and rights we are holding on to, and willingly lay down one of them for the sake of someone else. Then the mind of Christ Jesus will grow within us.
d250.pr: Today, quietly set aside one thing you could take credit for, and lift up someone else instead.

d251.t: The True Purpose of the Bestowal
msg: The seventh section of Paper 128 covers Jesus’ twenty-sixth year. During this period Jesus was watching his younger brothers and sisters marry and preparing to lay down, one by one, his responsibilities to the family. In the middle of this account of family affairs, today’s passage pauses to remind us clearly of the prime mission of Jesus’ seventh bestowal.

The passage says there is a fact we must never lose sight of: the prime mission of Jesus in his seventh bestowal was the acquirement of creature experience, the achievement of the sovereignty of Nebadon. Many people think that Jesus came to earth solely to atone for sin. But The Urantia Book teaches that his bestowal was, above all, for the experience of living a creature’s life firsthand. The passage goes on to say that in the gathering of this very experience he made the supreme revelation of the Paradise Father to Urantia and to his entire local universe. In other words, Jesus lived a human life to the full and at the same time revealed the Father. The very way he lived, doing the Father’s will, was itself a revelation of what the Father is like. Experience and revelation came together in a single life.

The passage adds that, incidental to these purposes, he also undertook to untangle the complicated affairs of this planet as they were related to the Lucifer rebellion. Settling the rebellion was important, but it was an incidental purpose. In this way The Urantia Book helps us understand Jesus’ mission in several layers: the achievement of sovereignty through experience, the revelation of the Father, and the resolution of the rebellion. This perspective lets us see Jesus’ Nazareth years in a new light. Those ordinary years in which he worked as a carpenter, supported his family, settled his brothers’ and sisters’ quarrels, and helped prepare their weddings were by no means unrelated to his mission. On the contrary, they were the heart of his prime mission, the acquiring of creature experience. Passing through every phase of ordinary life, he came to know human beings through and through.

And this gives deep meaning to our own ordinary lives. If the years Jesus spent caring for his family were part of a universe mission, then the time we spend in daily life is by no means trivial either. Our experience, too, is transformed with the Thought Adjuster into eternal values and contributes to the growth of the Supreme Being (see Paper 117). This passage also widens the way we look at Jesus. He is not merely one who paid a price for us; he is one who lived our life himself. He knows our joys and sorrows, our toil and disappointments, by experience. So when we come to him, we can be sure we are understood.

Let us also remember the way Jesus revealed the Father. He revealed him chiefly not by sermons or miracles but by his life. We too can reveal the Father more by our lives than by our words. The daily life of a person who lives with love, honesty, and patience becomes in itself a small revelation reflecting the character of the heavenly Father. Our lives also have a prime purpose and incidental purposes. When our hearts are caught up in many things, it is easy to forget what matters most. Amid countless tasks, Jesus never forgot his prime mission of doing the Father’s will and gathering experience.

Today, let us think again about what the most important purpose of our life is. And remembering that each ordinary day is a time of experience in which that purpose is being fulfilled, let us live faithfully.
d251.pr: Write down the most important purpose of your life in one sentence, and look back on today in its light.

d252.t: A Life That Did Not Seek Notice
msg: Paper 129 tells of Jesus’ later adult life, the period in which he left his Nazareth family, built boats in Capernaum, stayed in Jerusalem, and traveled the Mediterranean. The third section covers his twenty-ninth year and introduces his journey through the Mediterranean world, including Rome. Within that travel narrative, today’s passage sets out a principle we must keep in mind whenever we interpret Jesus’ life.

The passage says that in all our efforts to decipher the meaning of Jesus’ life on Urantia, we must be mindful of the motivation of the Michael bestowal. Many of his doings may appear strange. Why did he live quietly and ordinarily for so many years? Why did he not reveal himself on his Mediterranean journey? To understand the reason, we must discern the purpose of his sojourn on our world. The passage explains Jesus’ attitude in keeping with that purpose: he was consistently careful not to build up an overattractive and attention-consuming personal career. He wanted to make no unusual or overpowering appeals to his fellow men. Rather than drawing people’s attention to himself, he sought to help them discover the heavenly Father for themselves.

Why was this so? The passage says that he was devoted to two things. One was the work of revealing the heavenly Father to his fellow mortals; the other was the sublime task of living his mortal earth life all the while subject to the will of the same Father. Had he overwhelmed people with extraordinary powers, they would have been captivated by those powers instead of by the Father, and his life could not have been an example that ordinary human beings could follow. This reveals a profound principle of revelation. True revelation does not overpower people; it invites them. Miracles and marvels arouse a passing wonder, but they do not produce spiritual growth. Because Jesus respected people’s freedom to believe, he wanted them to come to the Father not through compelled amazement but through genuine understanding.

During his Mediterranean journey Jesus met a great many people, took an interest in their lives, gave them personal help, and planted seeds of truth in their hearts. Yet he did not reveal who he was, nor did he gather crowds. Those encounters were quiet, but their influence on people’s lives was deep and lasting. This teaching offers an important lesson for our life of faith today. We sometimes want to display our faith and be recognized for it. We feel the temptation to boast of our spiritual experiences or to appear more devout than others. But the way of Jesus was not to reveal himself but to reveal the Father.

This principle also applies when we help others. True help does not make others dependent on us; it helps them discover God for themselves and grow. The best service is the kind that leads people to remember God rather than us. A life that goes unnoticed is a humble life, but never a meaningless one. Jesus’ hidden years were no less important than his public ministry, and through that period he offered every phase of ordinary human life to the Father.

Today, let us too lay down the desire to show ourselves off and live a life that shows forth the Father. It is through quiet kindness and sincere interest that the love of the heavenly Father is most clearly conveyed.
d252.pr: Today, quietly help someone without telling anyone, and offer that deed to the Father alone.

msg: The last section of Paper 129 deals with the man Jesus. Having finished his Mediterranean journey, the twenty-nine-year-old Jesus had become a mature man who had experienced nearly every phase of human life. He knew both joy and sorrow, had lived through every stage of human life from birth to adulthood, and had experienced even the high stage of reconciliation between a human being and the Thought Adjuster. Today’s passage gives us the final verdict on the life he had lived.

The passage first acknowledges a frank fact. This perfect life which he lived in the likeness of mortal flesh did not receive the unqualified and universal approval of his fellow mortals, those who chanced to be his contemporaries on earth. Even his family did not fully understand him; the people of his hometown, Nazareth, rejected him; and the religious leaders condemned him. By human reckoning, his was a life that met with much misunderstanding and opposition. But the passage then declares the decisive fact: the life which Jesus of Nazareth lived in the flesh and on Urantia did receive full and unqualified acceptance by the Universal Father. Human judgment and God’s judgment differed. The life that people rejected, the Father fully accepted.

Why did the Father accept that life? The passage says it was because that life achieved two things at one and the same time, and in one and the same personality-life. One was the fullness of the revelation of the eternal God to mortal man; the other was the presentation of perfected human personality to the satisfaction of the Infinite Creator. Jesus showed God to man, and at the same time showed how man can reach God.

These two aspects are the key to understanding Jesus’ life. From above to below he revealed God; from below to above he displayed perfected humanity. He was the Son of God and the Son of Man, and the two became wholly one in a single personality (see Paper 120, section 4). And so his life became a new and living way to God. This truth gives us great comfort and courage today. When we, too, try to live according to the Father’s will, we may not win the full understanding and approval of those around us. At times we will be misunderstood, ridiculed, and lonely. But the ultimate judge of our lives is not other people; it is the heavenly Father.

Of course, this does not mean we should ignore the opinions of others. Jesus always respected people and listened even to their criticism. But the center of his life lay not in human approval but in the Father’s will. So he was neither elated by praise nor crushed by blame. We are all too easily shaken by what others think of us. We rejoice when praised and lose heart when criticized, and we worry constantly about how we look in others’ eyes. But a life spent seeking human approval never finds satisfaction. Only a life that seeks to do the Father’s will gives deep peace. And the Father is not one who accepts only perfect lives. Jesus’ life was perfect, but the Father also lovingly accepts the life of every child who sincerely strives to do his will. Despite our mistakes and shortcomings, a sincere heart that seeks the Father brings him joy.

Today, let us set the standard of our lives anew. When we live seeking not the applause of people but the smile of the Father, not human approval but the Father’s will, we too, like Jesus, will walk the path of a life accepted by the heavenly Father.
d253.pr: Whenever others’ opinions weigh on you today, quietly ask how the Father sees you.

d254.t: The Wisdom of Wheat and Tares
msg: Jesus’ conversation with Gadiah, the young Philistine, on the seashore at Joppa answers an age-old question: why does a good God permit evil in the world? Jesus does not regard evil as a reality that God himself created. What the Father gave is the power to choose between truth and error, and wherever there is freedom of choice there arises, along with it, the possibility of going against the way of light and life, that is, potential evil. Yet this possibility is no more than a shadow until an intelligent creature actually chooses the wrong way.

This passage clearly distinguishes evil from sin. A wrong choice makes the errors of evil real, and when the choice is made knowingly, deliberately, and in rebellion, it is exalted into sin. In the discourse on reality in the same Paper, Jesus likewise describes error as the penalty of imperfection and sin as conscious rebellion against spiritual reality. So we need not torment ourselves by condemning our weaknesses and mistakes as sin straightaway, but we must earnestly examine any choice by which we knowingly turn our backs on the light. The teaching that the possibility of evil is necessary to moral choice, but that actual evil need not exist (see Paper 132), belongs to the same line of thought.

Jesus then offers the parable of the wheat and the tares. The reason the Father permits the good and the evil to go along together until the end of life is not indifference but respect for the free will of his creatures. Goodness that is coerced is not true goodness. The Father wants us to choose the good for ourselves and to grow through that choosing. The Father’s patience in waiting until the harvest is also a mercy that gives us time to turn around.

This teaching also changes the way we look at the world. When we see injustice and wrongdoing around us, we feel the urge to rush in and pull up the tares. But the Father’s way is first to examine our own choices rather than judge others, and to walk the path that overcomes evil with good. Faced with the fact that evil exists, the response of the believer is not to despair or to doubt God’s goodness, but to choose the light in every moment of choice that is set before us.

This answer of Jesus shows how God’s sovereignty and human freedom can stand together. If the Father had removed every possibility of evil in advance, we would never have done evil, but neither could we ever have chosen the good out of love. A being without choice is like a machine, and a machine cannot share a fellowship of love with the Father. What the Father desires is not servants who obey under compulsion but sons and daughters who freely do his will. The possibility of evil, then, is not God’s failure but the price of the great love that created free personalities. When we grasp this, we no longer take our freedom lightly, and we come to regard using that freedom to answer the Father’s love as the highest honor of our lives.

Today, too, we stand before countless choices, great and small. Shall I speak the truth or evade it? Shall I be kind or indifferent? Shall I forgive or hold on to resentment? Each one of these sets the direction of our soul. The freedom to choose is a weighty responsibility and, at the same time, the greatest evidence that the Father respects us as true personalities. Let us resolve anew each day to use that freedom in walking the way of light and life.
d254.pr: Look back on today’s choices for any moment when you knowingly turned from the light, and choose the good again in that very place.

msg: On a hillside in Crete, Jesus met a young man gripped by fear and discouragement. Unable to get along with his companions, he was brooding over his misfortunes and trying to run away from the world. Jesus first awakened him to his strong body and clear mind and, above all, to the spirit that lived within him; then, in this passage, he extends the decisive invitation: this day you are to be reborn. This is not a promise for some distant future but a decision that can be made this very day.

The rebirth Jesus speaks of is neither a mystical rite nor a passing emotional outburst. It is a readjustment that moves the center of life from fear to faith, from self-pity to courage, and from self-protection to devoted service to man. What is remarkable is the word that when we become so readjusted to life within ourselves, we become likewise readjusted to the universe. When we attune our minds to the Father’s will, the great and real things of the universe are on our side. As Jesus said just before this, the sun rises on us every morning just as it salutes the most powerful of men.

In the life of one who is born of the spirit, the same events take on an entirely different meaning. Trouble invigorates, disappointment spurs one on, difficulties challenge, and obstacles stimulate. It is not the circumstances that have changed but the attitude of the soul that meets them. The spirit within us seeks to make our minds not the miserable slaves of fear but courageous allies in solving the problems of life. Faith is the key that sets that indwelling spirit free from the shackles of fear.

Jesus tells the young man to hasten back to duty. Being reborn is not a withdrawal from the world but a new entry into it. To live as one dedicated to the ennobling service of man on earth and destined to the superb and eternal service of God in eternity, this is what sonship with God really looks like. This young man, Fortune, later became a leader of the believers in Crete, which shows well how a single sincere decision can transform an entire life.

What is worth noticing in this scene is that Jesus did not make light of the young man’s suffering. He frankly acknowledged that those problems were real and could not be escaped as long as one lives. Yet instead of avoiding them, he urged him to set his mind to work at solving them. True faith is not a painkiller that lets us turn away from reality but a source of courage that enables us to face it squarely. The Thought Adjuster within us does not so much take our difficulties away as guide us beyond fear toward higher choices. Rebirth is a decision made once and for all and, at the same time, a decision repeated every day to choose faith instead of fear. If you fell yesterday, you can rise again today; if you wavered today, you can take hold of the Father’s hand again tomorrow.

There are days when we, too, want to shrink back and run away. On such days, let us remember these words. Our past failures do not define us. Today we can be re-established as people of faith, courage, and service. When we refuse to be ruled by fear and hold fast to the consciousness of being God’s children, a new love for our fellows will fill our souls and will overcome even our fear of other people. A life reborn each day is a life of victorious accomplishment.
d255.pr: Write down one fear that makes you shrink back, and then, rising above it, willingly carry out one duty today.

msg: Paper 131 is the record that Ganid, under Jesus’ guidance, compiled by gathering teachings about the Universal Deity from the scriptures of the world’s religions. Jesus taught him to respect the light of truth already dwelling within each religion, and through this work Ganid discovered that every people, in its own way, had been groping after the one God. This passage is drawn from the teachings of Judaism and holds the essence of the Hebrew psalms and wisdom literature.

The first sentence is the heart of the passage: the Lord is near all who call upon him in sincerity and in truth. The condition for drawing near to God is not a particular lineage or ritual but a true and sincere heart. And God promises, “⟦Q 131:2.9⟧If you seek me, you shall find me if you search for me with all your heart.⟦/Q⟧” As The Urantia Book teaches again and again, sincerely seeking God is never in vain. When we begin to seek the Father, the Father has already been seeking us (see Paper 131, section 10).

The words “⟦Q 131:2.9⟧weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning⟦/Q⟧” are a great comfort to those in the midst of trouble. Faith does not deny sorrow. The night is real, and the tears are real. But the person of faith knows that the night is not the last word. As it is written, “⟦Q 131:2.9⟧a merry heart does good like a medicine⟦/Q⟧”; the cheerfulness that springs from trust in God has power to heal both soul and body.

This passage also makes clear the moral order of the universe. Whoever sows iniquity shall reap calamity; they who sow the wind shall reap the whirlwind. No good thing will God withhold from those who walk uprightly. This is not a calculation of rewards and punishments but an assurance that the universe was made righteous. The words “⟦Q 131:2.9⟧the meek shall inherit the earth⟦/Q⟧” are also a truth that Jesus later taught his apostles again on the mountain (see Paper 140).

The words “⟦Q 131:2.9⟧Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man⟦/Q⟧” are also worth taking to heart. Here fear means not terror but the deep reverence and love we feel before the One who is great. Jesus later transformed the religion of fear into a religion of love, but he did not ask us to give up seriousness and humility before God. Keeping the commandments, likewise, is not the observance of outward rules but the expression of a heart that wants to do the Father’s will. In having Ganid gather these passages, Jesus intended to honor the heights of truth the Hebrew prophets had already reached, while letting that truth come to full flower within a relationship with the living Father. When we read the words of ancient scriptures, we too must hear, beyond the letters, the voice of the Father calling us today.

What we have to learn today is simple. God is not far away. When we call upon him sincerely, he is near. Whatever night we may be passing through, morning will surely come. While we wait for that morning, we need only walk uprightly, sow what is good, and seek him with all our heart. May we follow the generous gaze of Jesus, who helped Ganid find this truth even in the scriptures of other religions, and become people who honor the light that dwells in our neighbors’ faith as well. The very moment we call upon the Father in sincerity and in truth, he is already near us. Trusting in that nearness, let us walk today’s road with courage.
d256.pr: Tell the Father honestly about the night you are passing through now, and offer a prayer of trust as you wait for the joy of morning.

d257.t: The Heart That Feels After God
msg: The last section of Paper 131, under the heading “Our Religion,” is Ganid’s confession of what he had come to believe about God through Jesus’ teaching, after his study of the world’s religions. The fragments of truth gathered from many scriptures came together, in the life and words of Jesus, into a single living faith. This passage stands at the very center of that confession and portrays the character of the heavenly Father most warmly.

The first sentence is an astonishing promise: the Father in heaven will not suffer a single child on earth to perish if that child has a desire to find the Father and truly longs to be like him. Eternal survival is not a reward for blameless conduct; it depends on sincere desire and longing, that is, on the response of faith. Our Father even loves the wicked and is always kind to the ungrateful. His love is not measured out in proportion to our merits.

Ganid confesses that if more human beings could only know about the goodness of God, they would certainly be led to repent of their evil ways. This is the heart of Jesus’ teaching. What changes people at the root is not fear but knowing the goodness of God. All good things come down from the Father of light, in whom there is no variableness neither shadow of changing. The unchanging goodness of the Father is the anchor of our unsteady lives.

Especially worth taking to heart is the confession that when men begin to feel after God, that is evidence that God has found them. Because the spirit of the true God, the Thought Adjuster, is in man’s heart, the longing for God that arises within us is in fact a response to the call of the One who dwells within us (see Papers 107 and 108). We live in God and God dwells in us. And so the journey of seeking God is never a road we walk alone.

What makes Ganid’s confession all the more precious is that it is not a doctrine borrowed from others but a conviction he gained by seeking, comparing, and experiencing for himself. Having organized the teachings of the world’s religions after long labor, he goes on to confess that he had come to believe in God not merely, in a vague way, as the Father of all peoples, but as his own Father. Faith exerts its living power when it becomes, in this way, not someone else’s but our own. Jesus did not instill answers into Ganid; he opened the way for him to discover the truth for himself. We too must be able to confess, beyond the God we have read about in books and the God we have heard of from others, the Father we have met in our own lives. That confession need not be grand. If you can honestly say where today you tasted the goodness of the Father, that is the very beginning of your own religion.

If your faith feels vague and God seems far away, treasure that vague longing itself. That longing is already a sign that the Father is seeking you. And as the words say, he intends that all men should be brothers, so the way of seeking God is bound up as one with the way of treating our neighbors as brothers. May this be a day on which we seek the Father by following the longing within us and share his love with our brothers and sisters. Each of our small and clumsy steps toward the Father is to him the most welcome response of all. Let us not stop taking those steps.
d257.pr: Notice the small longing for God that stirs within you, and gratefully acknowledge it as the Father’s call.

msg: In Rome, Jesus held a deep conversation about truth and faith with Nabon, a high priest of the Mithraic cult. This passage, from that conversation, explains what faith does. Faith acts to release the superhuman activities of the divine spark, the immortal germ, that lives within the mind of man. That spark is the Thought Adjuster sent by the Universal Father, and it is the potential of our eternal survival.

Jesus compares ways of surviving. Plants and animals continue in time by passing on particles of themselves to the next generation. But the human soul passes beyond death by an altogether different path. It survives by identity association with the indwelling spark of divinity, that is, by becoming one with the Thought Adjuster. Our eternal future depends not on our bodies or our descendants but on our relationship with the spirit that dwells within us.

The words “⟦Q 132:3.6⟧the concealed seed of the human soul is an immortal spirit⟦/Q⟧” reveal the depth of our being. A seed buried in the ground is unseen, yet it holds within it the potential of an entire tree. So it is with our souls. Though they may look weak and imperfect now, they contain the pattern of a growth that will reach all the way to Paradise. Just as there are sunlight and water to awaken a seed, it is faith that awakens this seed. In the passage just before this one, Jesus said that truth cannot become a human possession without the exercise of faith.

The second generation of the soul is said to be the first of a succession of personality manifestations of spiritual and progressing existences. Life after death is not a break but a continuation. The growth of the soul begun on this earth goes on in the mansion worlds and at higher levels of the universe, and that journey ends only when it reaches the Universal Father, the source of all personality (see Paper 112). So every decision of faith we make today is a first step on an eternal journey.

It is worth reflecting a little further here on the relationship between the soul and the Adjuster. The Adjuster is a divine gift, perfect and immortal from the beginning, but the soul is a new reality that grows through the moral decisions and spiritual choices we make. The Adjuster does not trespass on our freedom; when we cooperate by faith, he unfolds his superhuman activities to the full. Survival, then, is not given automatically; it comes about when our will chooses to become one with the indwelling spirit. As the next passage says, human life continues because it has the task of finding God. Seeking God is not a hobby for religious people but the fundamental purpose of human existence, and as we walk toward that purpose, our souls grow a little more like eternity each day.

This teaching gives deep meaning to ordinary daily life. We spend much of our time meeting the needs of the body, but what truly lasts is the spiritual value that grows within the soul. Small acts of praying, loving truth, and serving our neighbors make the immortal seed grow. When we live today mindful of the divine spark within us, even ordinary tasks such as kitchen work and office work become linked with eternity. The seed within us may look small, but the One who planted it is the eternal Father, and he never abandons midway a work he has begun. So let us not be discouraged by our slow growth, but water that seed with faith again today.
d258.pr: Remembering the immortal seed within you, choose one act of faith that will help it grow, and carry it out today.

msg: During his six months in Rome, Jesus not only taught religious leaders but also met countless ordinary people in the streets, in the markets, and in their homes. This passage tells us what lay at the heart of that personal ministry. Always the burden of his message was the fact of the heavenly Father’s love and the truth of his mercy, coupled with the good news that man is a faith-son of this same God of love. Whomever he met and whatever the situation, this center never wavered.

Jesus’ method is remarkable. He did not teach one-sidedly but drew people into conversation by asking them questions. The interview would usually begin by his asking them questions and end by their asking him questions. This means that he respected the other person not as an object of teaching but as a personality capable of discovering truth for himself. To those he taught the most, he said the least. True teaching lies not in the quantity of words but in helping understanding to arise within the other person.

Those who derived most benefit from Jesus’ ministry were the overburdened, the anxious, and the dejected. They gained the opportunity to unburden their souls to a sympathetic and understanding listener. When someone truly listens to us, we are already half healed. Jesus did not stop at listening; he offered practical and immediately helpful suggestions, while not neglecting to speak words of present comfort. He cared for both the practical problems and the needs of the soul.

And always, at the end, he would tell them about the love of God and remind them that they were the children of the heavenly Father. Practical help and spiritual truth were never kept apart. This is why Jesus’ ministry changed people’s lives at the root. Solving problems alone does not renew the soul, and words of comfort alone do not change a life. Jesus bound the two together and served the whole person. The very next passage tells us that he made such contacts with more than five hundred people in Rome.

This attitude of Jesus shows how deeply he loved people. Whether he was talking with a high-ranking senator in the capital of the world or defending a poor man who had been falsely accused, he treated each with the same interest and respect. He did not divide people by class or usefulness but saw them all as children of the Father. Nor did he reveal his identity or astonish people with miracles. As an ordinary man, using ordinary means, asking, listening, helping, and encouraging, he sowed the seeds of truth in people’s souls. This is a path all of us can follow. Even without special talents or position, sincere interest and attentive listening are gifts of love that anyone can give.

We too can learn this way. If someone we meet today is weary, let us first ask and listen rather than give advice. Let us look for some small thing that will help with that person’s real difficulty and, if we can, convey by word or manner that he or she is a beloved child of God. Jesus showed that the greatest and most effective ministry to people is accomplished through personal contact with one person at a time. To treat one person with sincerity is itself the work of the kingdom.
d259.pr: Today, offer a question to someone who is weary before giving any advice, and take the time to hear their story all the way through.

msg: While Jesus and Ganid were staying in Corinth, Jesus met many kinds of people and left each a brief word suited exactly to him. To the miller, the Roman centurion, the judge, the innkeeper’s wife, and even a condemned criminal, those words are jewels of personal ministry that pierce to the heart of a person’s situation. This passage is what he said to a boy who had run away from home and was drifting about. Jesus neither scolded the boy nor forced him to return home, but gently and clearly awakened him to the truth he had to face.

The words “⟦Q 133:4.11⟧there are two things you cannot run away from — God and yourself⟦/Q⟧” are simple yet profound. We may change places, change companions, and change our surroundings, but we still take ourselves along with us. The fears and wounds in our hearts and our unresolved problems follow us just the same to a new place. Many people try to solve their problems by leaving when life is hard, but real change begins not outside but within. The runaway boy may have thought he would be free once he left home, but the discontent and fear he was trying to escape remained in his heart and set out on the road with him.

Yet these words also hold great comfort. The other one from whom we cannot run away is God. Jesus says, wherever you may go, you take with you the spirit of the heavenly Father which lives within your heart. However far we may flee, the Thought Adjuster never leaves us. Wherever the boy went, he was not alone. This fact is a warning and, at the same time, the greatest reassurance, for the One who knows us best is always with us.

Jesus goes on to say, stop trying to deceive yourself. Running away usually begins with self-deception. If we believe the problem lies only with other people or with our circumstances, we need never look at ourselves. Jesus urges the boy to settle down to the courageous practice of facing the facts of life. This is in the same vein as his teaching to the fear-ridden young man in Crete (see Paper 130). True faith is not a hiding place from reality but the power to overcome it. The honesty that refuses to deceive itself is the starting point of all spiritual growth. The moment we acknowledge the truth, room at last opens up for the Father’s help to work.

The source of that power is the assurance of sonship with God and the certainty of eternal life. When we lay hold of the fact that we are children of God, we can finally look at the reality of ourselves without fear. A beloved child need not hide his weaknesses. In the Father’s love we can rise again from where we have fallen and stand once more before the problems we wanted to avoid. Jesus tells the boy, from this day on purpose to be a real man. A decision is always a matter for today.

Each of us, too, lives carrying something we would rather avoid. It may be a reconciliation we have put off, a responsibility we have ignored, or a side of ourselves we would rather not look at. Today, honestly face one of them. When we take our stand there, the spirit of the heavenly Father stands there with us. To anyone determined to face life bravely and intelligently, the Father will add day by day the wisdom and courage that are needed.
d260.pr: Honestly write down one problem you have been avoiding, and decide on a first step toward facing it together with the Father.

msg: While staying in the mountains of Cyprus with Ganid, who had recovered from an illness, Jesus held a long conversation about the functions of the human mind. After teaching that self-consciousness is a reality, that ideas are not merely a record of sensations, and that the truly reflective human intellect is not wholly bound by the limitations of time, in this passage he concludes with the very practical subject of the unity of the mind: the human mind does not well stand the conflict of double allegiance.

It is a severe strain on the soul to undergo the experience of an effort to serve both good and evil. We often live walking a tightrope between two paths, outwardly following the right way while inwardly clinging to other desires. But such a life produces constant inner tension and drains the strength of the mind, and when such conflicts pile up unresolved, they may even end in mind disruption. Much of the anxiety and fatigue we suffer is rooted in precisely this divided allegiance. Jesus taught that no one can serve two masters, and this passage shows that those words are not only a moral command but also a truth about the health of the mind.

Jesus offers the answer clearly. The supremely happy and efficiently unified mind is the one wholly dedicated to the doing of the will of the Father in heaven. Unity of mind comes not from some technique for forcibly ordering our thoughts but from placing the supreme loyalty of our life in one place. Once the fundamental decision to do the Father’s will is made, our choices, great and small, begin to fall into order around that center. This was the secret of the life Jesus showed throughout his days. This decision is not made once and for all; it must be renewed every day, but the more often it is renewed, the more the mind is gathered into one and gains a quiet strength.

Here Jesus adds an important warning. Surrendering noble aspirations or compromising spiritual ideals in order to gain peace is no true solution. When conflict is painful, we are tempted to lower our standards and find calm the easy way. If we dull the voice of conscience, things may grow quiet for a while. But peace gained in that way does not foster the survival character of the soul. It is only a false calm bought at the price of giving up growth.

True peace is attained by the stalwart assertion of the triumph of that which is true, that is, by overcoming evil with the potent force of good. It means resolving the conflict in the mind not by compromising with evil but by choosing and doing the good more powerfully. Peace gained in this way is not easily shaken, and in the process the soul grows stronger and more beautiful. As Jesus taught in Rome, spiritual evolution is the experience of choosing the good more and more voluntarily, and the potential of evil diminishes accordingly (see Paper 132).

Today, look to see whether there is a conflict in your heart from trying to serve two masters. Do not try to cover it over by lowering your standards; instead, renew your decision to do the Father’s will. Then express that decision in one small good deed. When we serve the Father with an undivided heart, we live the happiest and most efficient of lives, and a peace that the world cannot give comes to dwell in our hearts. May that peace guard our hearts today.
d261.pr: Find one conflict that divides your heart, and overcome it with a good deed rather than by lowering your standards.

msg: In A.D. 24, Jesus’ thirtieth year, after he returned from his Mediterranean journey, was outwardly a quiet year. He settled his family’s affairs, blessed the marriages of his brothers and sisters, and prepared for a caravan trip to the Caspian Sea. But this passage tells us that beneath that ordinary surface something very special was taking place. Great progress was being made in the harmony between his human mind and the indwelling Thought Adjuster.

The Thought Adjuster had been actively engaged in reorganizing Jesus’ thinking and in rehearsing his mind for the great events to come. This shows that even Jesus, the Son of God, grew as a human being in cooperation with the Adjuster. He did not possess everything in completed form from the beginning. Just as we do, he sought the Father’s will day by day, listened to the guidance within, and attuned his mind to the leading of the Adjuster. The Urantia Book tells us that Jesus came to understand his mission little by little from his childhood, and that he skipped not a single step in the process of human growth. That is why his life is for us not a distant myth but a path we can follow.

The last sentence of this passage sums up the whole of Jesus’ life. He began life as God appearing as man, and he was now making ready to complete his earth career as man appearing as God. This transition is completed in his sojourn on Mount Hermon (Paper 134, section 8) and in his baptism in the Jordan (see Paper 136). When a human mind becomes wholly one with the divine spirit, God is revealed to the world through that human being. The voice from heaven at his baptism was the Father’s acknowledgment that this long preparation had borne fruit.

This is not a story unrelated to us. Jesus’ life is the pattern for the path every mortal is to walk. Within us, too, dwells a Thought Adjuster sent by the same Universal Father. The Adjuster little by little reorganizes our thinking and prepares our minds to be attuned to spiritual reality. The more we cooperate, the deeper the harmony between our human mind and the Adjuster becomes, until at last it reaches eternal fusion (see Papers 110 and 111).

What is worth noting is that this great inner change took place not in the midst of extraordinary events but in ordinary daily life. Jesus deepened his harmony with the Adjuster within while caring for his family, working, and traveling. Spiritual growth comes not by withdrawing from the world but by faithfully carrying out the duties of the world. A quiet and unremarkable year may in fact be a time of the deepest preparation. The ordinary days we spend laboring for our families and serving our neighbors become, for the Adjuster, precious material with which to shape us.

If your life now seems to flow on monotonously with nothing special happening, do not think of that time as wasted. In those quiet times the Thought Adjuster may be preparing you for what is to come. At the end of the day, sit quietly for a moment and look back on how far your thoughts and choices today were in harmony with the divine guide within you. That small act of reflection is the surest way to deepen that harmony.
d262.pr: At the end of the day, quietly reflect on whether your thoughts and choices today were in harmony with the Adjuster within you.

msg: On his way back from the Caspian Sea, Jesus gave lectures at the temple of religious philosophy at Urmia. Teachers of more than thirty religions and religious cults had gathered there together. Jesus taught these believers of many kinds about the sovereignty of God and the brotherhood of man, and this passage holds the core principle of those lectures: if different religions recognize the spirit sovereignty of God the Father, then will all such religions remain at peace.

This principle is simple, yet it runs through the whole of human history. Religious strife and persecution have usually arisen when one religion assumes that it alone is superior and possesses exclusive authority over all others. When people set not God but their own religious group in the highest place, faith turns into intolerance and neighbors become enemies. The countless tragedies carried out in the name of religion bear witness to this. The moment we believe that our religion alone has a monopoly on God, other people’s sincere faith appears not as something to respect but as an error to be eliminated. And so arises the contradiction of people who claim to serve the God of love spreading hatred instead.

The answer Jesus offered was not to make all religions the same. Rather, it was for all religions to recognize the sovereignty of the one Father who stands above them all. If God is the Father of all, then all who seek him are brothers. When there is the recognition that, though we walk different paths, we are all turned toward the same Father, differences become not a threat but a diversity that enriches one another. In the same Paper, this principle is extended further into the teaching on political sovereignty.

This is why the religionists of Urmia were able to live together in comparative peace and tranquillity. Earlier, while compiling the scriptures of the world’s religions with Ganid (see Paper 131), Jesus had set an example of respecting the light of truth dwelling in every religion. He despised no religion, but started from the truth each person already held and led them on to higher truth. Because true religion is a personal experience, it cannot be forced. His lectures at Urmia were not an occasion to champion any particular religion but an occasion to bring all believers before the one Father.

This teaching asks humility of us today. However precious the truth we have come to understand, neither our community of faith nor our interpretation can take the place of God himself. One who truly recognizes the sovereignty of God knows that he is not the owner of truth but a pilgrim seeking it. Such a person does not lose openness and respect even before neighbors of other faiths, and when speaking of his own faith, he shows it by his life rather than by pressure.

Today, when you meet someone of another religion or faith tradition, remember this principle. Before seeing that person as someone to persuade or as a rival, see him or her as a brother or sister feeling after the same Father. Look for the light of truth in that person’s faith from which you can learn. Respecting one another under the sovereignty of God, this is the path to true peace among the religions.
d263.pr: Think of one neighbor of another faith, and find one truth in that faith that you can honor.

d264.t: The One Who Comes After Me
msg: As John the Baptist journeyed north along the Jordan preaching, he thought much about Jesus. His disciples asked him again and again, “⟦Q 135:7.2⟧Are you the Messiah?⟦/Q⟧” In answer to that question, John first made reference at Adam to “⟦Q 135:7.2⟧another one who is to come after me.⟦/Q⟧” This passage shows John’s remarkable humility before the great multitudes who followed him. He confessed that there would come after him one greater than he, whose sandal straps he was not worthy to stoop down and unloose.

John was at that time the most famous preacher in Palestine. Multitudes flocked to receive his baptism, and many were inclined to regard him as the Messiah. In such a position, to lower oneself and lift up another is never easy. The human heart does not readily let go of recognition and influence. But John knew the essence of his mission. He was the herald who prepared the way, not the way itself. He did not claim the acclaim of the crowds as his own, but turned the eyes fixed on him toward the One who was to come.

John said, “⟦Q 135:7.2⟧I baptize you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.⟦/Q⟧” John’s baptism was a sign of repentance; it led people to turn their hearts and prepare to receive the kingdom of God. But true transformation comes not through outward ritual but through the spirit poured out within. The life of Jesus and the Spirit of Truth poured out afterward truly accomplished that spiritual baptism John had dimly foreseen (see Paper 194). Because John knew his role lay in preparation, he did not regard his own baptism as the final word.

Yet John’s message also carried the limitations of his age. The picture of judgment, of gathering the wheat and burning the chaff with fire, reflects the expectations of the apocalyptists of the time and the influence of Elijah. John still held confused ideas about the coming kingdom and its king. The kingdom Jesus actually revealed was a spiritual kingdom that rules human hearts by the love and mercy of the Father rather than by the fire of judgment. Even so, John remained faithful to the very end to as much light as he understood.

What we learn from John is precisely this faithfulness and humility. In a sense, all of us are people who prepare the way for others. Parents prepare the way for their children, teachers for their students, and elders in the faith for those who come after them. Those who do this well do not try to be the center of attention, but gladly step back so that others may grow greater. It is precisely in that place of self-emptying that the soul grows greatest. True service lies not in leaving one’s name behind but in doing one’s part so that God’s work may be accomplished and then gladly stepping aside. John showed in his own life what such service is.

Today, look back on whom your work is lifting up. Consider whether it is for your own recognition and influence, or for God and your neighbors. If you can sincerely rejoice in a moment when someone other than you shines more brightly, then you are walking the path of humility that John walked. Whoever walks that path tastes the true freedom of rejoicing in another’s growth as though it were one’s own.
d264.pr: Today, sincerely rejoice when someone else is recognized, and offer them a warm word that lifts them up.

msg: John the Baptist spent more than a year imprisoned by Herod Antipas in the fortress of Machaerus. He who had roamed the wilderness baptizing multitudes was now shut up in a dark prison, and the waiting was humanly unbearable. He may have expected Jesus to deliver him by his power. But nothing happened, and doubt crept into his heart. He sent messengers to ask Jesus, “⟦Q 135:11.4⟧Are you truly the Messiah?⟦/Q⟧”

John’s question honestly shows that even to a person of faith the night of doubt may come. The very John who had baptized Jesus in the Jordan and heard the voice from heaven was now wavering. His questions, “⟦Q 135:11.4⟧Is my work done? Why do I languish in prison?⟦/Q⟧” are also the questions of everyone who meets the silence of God in the midst of suffering. The Urantia Book does not hide this doubt. The mere fact that doubt has come is not a failure of faith. At such times we, like John, may ask honestly. The Father does not rebuke a sincere question.

Jesus’ reply holds deep love and, at the same time, a clear principle. He said he had not forgotten John, yet asked John to suffer him also this. Jesus had already decided in the wilderness not to use his superhuman power for personal ends or to rescue his own (see Paper 136). He did not bring John out of prison by a miracle. Instead he pointed to the fact that the poor were having good tidings preached to them, evidence that John’s labors had not been in vain. Between love for his friend and the will of the Father, Jesus chose the Father’s will.

And Jesus told the beloved herald of his earth mission that he shall be abundantly blessed in the age to come if he finds no occasion to doubt and stumble over him. This message greatly comforted John, did much to stabilize his faith, and gave him strength to meet the tragic death that was soon to come. His circumstances did not change, but John’s soul did. God’s answer does not always come in the way we want, but it never leaves out what we truly need.

This story teaches an important lesson about answered prayer. We pray for our suffering to be taken away, but the Father sometimes gives us, rather than removal of the suffering, the faith and comfort to endure it. This is not indifference but love that springs from greater wisdom and a longer view. Life on this earth is only the first stage of an eternal journey, and John’s true reward was awaiting him in the age to come. That inner faith can be established anew even when outward circumstances remain unchanged, this is the deepest gift God gives to his children in the midst of suffering.

If you now feel the silence of God in a situation like a prison, bring your doubt honestly to the Father, as John did. And look back on the good things already happening in your life, the fruit your labors have borne. The Father has never forgotten you. Even if your circumstances stay the same, the Father’s comfort will steady your faith and give you strength to meet with courage whatever may come.
d265.pr: Bring the doubt now in your heart honestly to the Father in prayer, and count one small fruit your labors have borne.

d266.t: The True Meaning of the Wilderness
msg: After his baptism in the Jordan, Jesus went into the hills of Perea and spent forty days alone. This period is often pictured as a time of hunger and temptation, but The Urantia Book presents an entirely different picture. This passage says plainly that Jesus did not go into retirement for the purpose of fasting and for the affliction of his soul. He was not an ascetic, and he came forever to destroy all such notions regarding the approach to God. This one sentence lifts a heavy burden that religious people have carried for countless generations.

Throughout humanity’s religious history, people long believed that they had to torment their bodies and abuse themselves in order to draw near to God. Penance, fasting, and self-denial were treated as the measure of holiness. But the God whom Jesus revealed is not one who demands the suffering of his children; he is a Father who delights in their trust and love. Our way to God is not the way of tormenting ourselves but the way of a sincere heart that seeks to know and do the Father’s will. Afflicting the soul does not raise anyone higher spiritually.

Why, then, did Jesus withdraw? Moses and Elijah, and even John the Baptist, also went into the wilderness, but Jesus’ reasons were entirely different from theirs. He was now wholly self-conscious of his relation to the universe of his making and to the universe of universes, supervised by the Paradise Father. And he now fully recalled the bestowal charge and its instructions given by his elder brother, Immanuel. He wanted to meditate quietly on these far-flung relationships and to think out the plans for his public labors in behalf of this world and all the other worlds of his local universe.

In other words, Jesus’ wilderness was a place not of self-mortification but of reflection and decision. As the later sections of the same Paper show, there he made a number of great decisions about how he would use his superhuman power, by what methods he would win people’s attention, and what kind of kingdom he would establish (see Paper 136, sections 5–10). Every one of those decisions turned toward following the Father’s will, toward walking the natural and ordinary way. What a person facing great work needs is not to afflict the body but time to quiet the mind and think things through with the Father.

This teaching applies directly to our own spiritual life. We too need time alone, time to think quietly and pray. But the purpose of that time is not to punish ourselves or to display our piety. It is to review the direction of our lives together with the Father and to plan wisely the road ahead. To step back for a while from the busyness of daily life and consider the relationships in which our life is set, and what we should put first before God, this is each person’s own small wilderness.

Today, make a place where you can stay quietly alone, even for a short while. Spend that time not in self-reproach or fear but with the peaceful heart of a child sitting before a loving Father. And bring one decision now before you to the Father and think it over together with him. Just as the decisions Jesus made in the hills guided his whole life, the decisions we make in stillness together with the Father will lead our lives along the right path.
d266.pr: Stay quietly alone for even a short time today, and calmly think through one decision before you together with the Father.

msg: The fourth decision Jesus made during his forty days in the wilderness concerned whether he would use his superhuman power to attract people’s attention or win their support. He knew better than anyone that by astonishing people with miracles and wonders he could quickly gather great crowds. He could have captivated a whole nation at a single stroke by dramatic means. But this passage tells us that Jesus chose to establish the kingdom of heaven in the hearts of mankind by natural, ordinary, difficult, and trying methods.

Why did Jesus refuse the easy shortcut? The earlier part of the same section explains that astonishing people with miracles stimulates material thinking and produces a merely outward loyalty. Faith gained through amazement easily cools unless there is ever greater amazement. But the kingdom of heaven must be built in the hearts of men, upon free choice and living faith. A belief that is forced or overwhelmed does not transform the soul. Because Jesus respected people’s personalities and freedom, he did not try to seize their hearts by force. True faith grows not from amazement but from conviction of truth and love for the Father.

What is especially moving in this passage is that the way Jesus chose was just such procedures as his earth children must subsequently follow in their work of enlarging and extending the kingdom. Jesus prepared the way not for himself alone but for all the believers who would follow. The way we share truth and love with our neighbors should be the same. We approach people’s hearts not with spectacular events or overpowering force but with sincerity in ordinary life and persevering love.

Jesus also knew that it would be “⟦Q 136:8.6⟧through much tribulation that many of the children of all ages would enter into the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” The way of faith is never smooth. Jesus did not choose a path free of difficulty for himself, nor did he promise his followers that they would have none. But in passing through those difficulties the soul is tempered, faith deepens, and the relationship with God grows firmer. In the end, not the easy way but the true way is the best way.

The last sentence reveals the heart of this decision. Jesus was passing through the great test of civilized man, to have power and steadfastly refuse to use it for purely selfish or personal purposes. Those who have power are always tempted to use it for their own convenience. We too have powers great and small, such as position and money, knowledge and influence. By possessing all power in heaven and on earth and yet not using it for himself, Jesus showed that true greatness lies in service. He came as one who serves, and his power was always used only for others.

Today we too stand before the temptation of shortcuts. There are times when we want to use dishonest means or the pressure of power to get things done quickly, to persuade people easily, or to have our own way. At such times, let us remember the way Jesus chose. Even if it is slow and difficult, choose the natural and honest way, the patient way that respects the freedom of others. That way may seem slow, but it builds in human hearts a kingdom that will never fall.
d267.pr: Look for one opportunity today to use whatever small power you have not for your own convenience but to serve someone else.

d268.t: A Long Night by the Lake
msg: After the water became wine at the wedding feast in Cana, Jesus’ heart was heavy. Because of that event people acclaimed him and believed him to be the Messiah, but Jesus was deeply perplexed that they believed in him only because of an unusual occurrence. That night, after returning to Capernaum, he could not sleep; donning his evening wraps, he went out to the lake shore and sat thinking until dawn. This passage tells us what Jesus came to understand in that long night of meditation. The scene shows how earnestly the Son of God pondered his mission with a human mind.

The problem Jesus faced was very complicated. The Jewish people were waiting for a political Messiah who would restore the throne of David and defeat Rome. But Jesus’ mission was not such a worldly kingdom; it was a spiritual kingdom established in human hearts. To accept the title of Messiah risked encouraging people’s mistaken expectations, yet to reject it altogether seemed likely to close off the way to proclaiming the message of the kingdom. In the midst of that tension he kept watch alone through the night, seeking a way forward.

That night Jesus came to see one thing clearly: he never would be able to make his followers see him in any other light than as the long-expected Messiah. He acknowledged that, though he was not the Davidic type of Messiah, he was truly the fulfillment of the prophetic utterances of the more spiritually minded of the olden seers. And so, from then on, never again did he wholly deny that he was the Messiah. While acknowledging the limits of people’s understanding, he found a way to proclaim the truth within them. This was not a compromise that bent the truth but the wisdom of love, which starts from where people stand and seeks to lead them on to higher truth.

And the most important conclusion was this: he decided to leave the final untangling of this complicated situation to the outworking of the Father’s will. Jesus did not try to solve every problem then and there. Having thought and decided as far as he could, he left the rest to the Father. This was not an irresponsible evasion but an expression of deep trust. When there are things that human wisdom cannot fully fathom, entrusting them to the Father’s hands is the wisest choice.

This picture of Jesus gives us great comfort. He, the Son of God, also wrestled and agonized through the night as a human being. He did not walk along at ease, knowing all the answers in advance; like us, he sought his way by thinking deeply and praying before hard problems. So when we spend sleepless nights over problems whose answers are not easily seen, it is not because our faith is lacking. Such a night can become a precious time of seeking the way together with the Father. Learning, after much struggle, to entrust things to the Father is the very maturity of faith.

If there is a complicated problem weighing on your heart now, try doing as Jesus did. In a quiet place, look at the problem honestly and distinguish what you can do from what you cannot. Make courageously the decisions that are yours to make, and leave to the Father’s will the parts you cannot solve by your own strength. Into the heart of one who entrusts things in this way, peace comes with the light of dawn, and new strength springs up for living the next day.
d268.pr: Take one problem that weighs on your heart, and write down separately what is yours to do and what you will leave to the Father.

d269.t: A Kingdom Not of This World
msg: In June of A.D. 26, Jesus preached his first full public sermon on the kingdom of God in the synagogue at Capernaum. This sermon was a landmark proclamation announcing the start of his public career. Many were waiting with bated breath to hear what kind of kingdom the Messiah would set up. In this passage Jesus proclaims a kingdom entirely different from what they expected. That kingdom is not established by armies and a throne of power; it is a spiritual kingdom established through the spirit of the Father indwelling human minds and through the Spirit of Truth.

Jesus says that the Father in heaven sends his spirit to indwell the minds of men. This is a teaching about the Thought Adjuster. And he foretells that when he has finished his work on earth, the Spirit of Truth shall be poured out upon all flesh. This promise was fulfilled at Pentecost (see Paper 194). The spirit of the Father and the Spirit of Truth, these two divine presences, establish believers in the kingdom of spiritual understanding and divine righteousness. The foundation of the kingdom is not an outward institution but the spirit within us. In a sense, the seed of that kingdom has already been planted in each one of us.

The declaration “⟦Q 137:8.7⟧My kingdom is not of this world⟦/Q⟧” came as a great shock to the people of that time. They wanted a leader who would defeat Rome and restore the glory of Israel. But Jesus said plainly that the Son of Man will not lead forth armies in battle for the establishment of a throne of power. He is the Prince of Peace, the revelation of the everlasting Father. The decisions he made in the wilderness (see Paper 136) are clearly displayed in this first public sermon.

How, then, does one enter this kingdom? The children of this world fight for the establishment and enlargement of the kingdoms of this world, but Jesus’ disciples enter the kingdom of heaven by their moral decisions and by their spirit victories. The battlefield of the kingdom is not the outer world but our own hearts. The decision to overcome selfishness and choose love, the decision to overcome fear and choose faith, the decision to overcome hatred and choose forgiveness, these are the very doors into the kingdom. These victories are won not by the sword but by the fruits of the spirit. As these small daily decisions accumulate, they shape our souls into citizens of the kingdom.

And when they once enter therein, they shall find joy, righteousness, and eternal life. This is not merely a reward in the distant future. Those who have entered the kingdom taste joy here and now, grow in righteousness, and have already begun eternal life. The kingdom of heaven is not a place but a living relationship with God, and within that relationship the quality of our lives is fundamentally changed. Those who were waiting for political liberation were disappointed, but those who found liberation of heart discovered true freedom.

Today we too need to look at what we are pursuing, the kingdoms of this world or the kingdom of heaven. Have we forgotten the kingdom within while fighting for success, position, and possessions? Each small moral decision we make today can be a step into the kingdom of heaven. In those decisions the spirit of the Father and the Spirit of Truth will establish us firmly and give us a joy the world cannot give. The kingdom of heaven is not far off; it begins in our choices today.
d269.pr: In a moment of conflict today, make one small moral decision to choose love instead of selfishness.
